title: Lecture 16 – Optic nerve
html:
Source: c16 optic nerve.pptx – 22 slides

Optic Nerve #1

Diseases #2

  • optic neuropathies.
  • Etiology
  • inflammatory
  • ischemic
  • toxic
  • edematous,
  • atrophic

Inflammatory optic neuropathies #3

  • segments of the optic nerve
  • anterior (juxtabulbar)
  • posterior (retrobulbar)

Anterior inflammatory optic neuropathy (papillitis) #4

  • Symptoms.
  • depression of the sight
  • misty vision
  • Central visual field defects
  • Signs
  • papilla is congested with indistinct margins,
  • edema of the optic disk spreading upon the nearby retina
  • on the papilla
  • exudates and hemorrhages appear
  • engorgement and tortuosity of the central vessels

Anterior inflammatory optic neuropathy papillitis #5

  • Etiology
  • systemic infectious diseases (scarlet fever, typhoid fever, influenza, meningitis, erysipelas etc);
  • orbital cellulitis;
  • sinusitis; dental foci, tonsillitis.
  • Treatment
  • etiological
  • corticosteroids locally (subconjunctival or retrobulbar injections)
  • antibiotics and corticosteroids systemically.

Posterior inflammatory optic neuropathy(retrobulbar optic neuropathy or retrobulbar optic neuritis) #6

  • Symptoms
  • abrupt diminishing the vision with pains within the depth of the orbit, that accentuate by movements of the ocular globe
  • the eye is tender to touch
  • visual field presents central scotoma, initially for red and green colours
  • Signs
  • ocular fundus is initially normal
  • after 3-4 weeks pallor of the temporal part of the papilla or even of the whole optic disk .

Posterior inflammatory optic neuropathy #7

  • Etiology.
  • demyelinating diseases (multiple sclerosis);
  • optic neuromyelitis;
  • sinus inflammations (especially ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses);
  • focal infections (dental foci, tonsil),
  • viral infections.
  • Treatment
  • etiological
  • corticosteroids and antibiotics systemically
  • corticosteroids locally (subconjunctival or retrobulbar injections)

Ischemic optic neuropathies #8

  • anterior
  • posterior
  • segments of the optic nerve

Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy pseudopapillitis #9

  • involves juxtabulbar portion of the optic nerve
  • Symptoms and signs
  • similar to those of papillitis
  • Etiology
  • occurs in elderly patients
  • occlusion of the vessels that nourish the anterior segment of the optic nerve posterior long ciliary artery
  • arteriosclerosis (in more than 80% of cases)
  • Horton’s disease (cranial arteritis)
  • Treatment
  • similar to papillitis

Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy #10

  • Horton’s disease
  • Etiology:
  • Giant cell arteritis
  • frequently bilateral granulomatous vasculitis that primarily affects the medium-sized and small arteries.
  • the temporal arteries,
  • ophthalmic artery,
  • short posterior ciliary arteries,
  • central retinal artery,
  • the proximal portion of the vertebral arteries,

Symptoms: #11

  • sudden unilateral blindness or severe visual impairment.
  • headaches, painful scalp in the region of the temporal arteries,
  • tenderness to palpation in the region of the temporal arteries, pain while chewing (a characteristic sign),
  • weight loss, reduced general health and exercise tolerance.
  • history of amaurosis fugax or polymyalgia rheumatica.

Diagnostic considerations: #12

  • ophthalmoscopic the same as in arteriosclerotic AION
  • Other
  • increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • the most important finding
  • increased level of C-reactive protein,
  • leukocytosis, iron-deficiency anemia.
  • The temporal arteries are prominent painful to palpation, and have no pulse.
  • biopsy of the temporal artery.

Treatment: #13

  • high-dosage systemic steroid
  • to protect the fellow eye
  • reduced as the ESR decreases, C-reactive protein levels drop, and clinical symptoms abate.
  • maintenance dose required for several months
  • pentoxifylline

Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (retrobulbar) #14

  • involves the (retrobulbar) segment of the optic nerve
  • Symptoms and signs
  • similar to retrobulbar inflammatory optic neuropathy
  • Etiology
  • occlusion of the vessels of the retrobulbar segment of the optic nerve branches of the central retinal artery or ophthalmic artery,
  • arteriosclerosis
  • Horton’s diseases
  • Treatment
  • similar to inflammatory optic neuropathy

Toxical optic neuropathies #15

  • Symptoms and signs
  • similar to papillitis or retrobulbar optic neuritis
  • depending upon the segment of the optic nerve involved (anterior or posterior )
  • Etiology
  • endogenous
  • diabetes, pregnancy,
  • exogenous
  • antituberculous drugs (ethambutol);
  • persons smoking the pipe shag tobacco;
  • accidental use of methyl alcohol,
  • chronic use of ethyl alcohol.
  • Treatment
  • Etiological
  • Corticosteroids sistemic and local (injections)
  • Vitamins group B,diuretics
  • stopping the use of toxical substances.

Edematous optic neuropathy (papilla edema) #16

  • Signs and symptoms
  • a sign of heightened intracranial pressure associated or not with other signs and symptoms
  • headaches, vomiting, nausea, vertigo and oculomotor nerve pareses or paralyses
  • Bilateral
  • margins are highlighted and indistinct resembling a jelly fish or chrysanthemum flower.
  • sight and visual field are normal for a long period of time
  • diminishing the visual acuity if atrophy of the papilla occur.

Edematous optic neuropathy (papilla edema) #17

  • Signs and symptoms
  • a sign of heightened intracranial pressure associated or not with other signs and symptoms
  • headaches, vomiting, nausea, vertigo and
  • oculomotor nerve pareses or paralyses
  • edema of the papilla (papilloedema) whose margins are highlighted and indistinct resembling a jelly fish or a chrysanthemum flower.
  • sight and visual field are normal for a long period of time
  • diminishing the visual
  • atrophy of the papilla occur.

Edematous optic neuropathy (papilla edema) #18

  • Differential diagnosis
  • papillitis
  • sight and visual field are impaired since the beginning the disease
  • Etiology
  • (1) intracranial tumors of the posterior brain;
  • (2) meningitis;
  • (3) cranio-orbital trauma;
  • (4) subarachnoidal hemorrhage.
  • Treatment
  • Surgery immediately after diagnosing a space occupying lesion
  • medical diseases have to be etiologically treated.

Optic nerve atrophies #19

  • a status following a lot of diseases.
  • Symptoms
  • progressive depression of the vision
  • concentrical shrinkages of the visual field
  • Signs
  • optic disk
  • Pallor (white)
  • diffuse or sectorial (marked on the temporal side)
  • No elevation
  • well contoured

Optic nerve atrophies #20

  • Clinical forms. (etiology) :
  • primary atrophy.
  • neuro-syphylis, demyelinating diseases,
  • retrobulbar neuritis,
  • secondary atrophy.
  • (1) lesions of the optic canal during cranial trauma
  • (2) tumors that compress the optic pathways (pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngioma)

Optic nerve atrophies #21

  • Clinical forms. (etiology) :
  • post papillitis atrophy
  • The optic disk becomes pale once the edema of the papilla has subsided.
  • after edematous optic neuropathy.
  • Should the edema last long time (>6 months)
  • vascular atrophy.
  • after an ischemic optic neuropathy
  • glaucomatous atrophy.
  • during the evolution of vaying forms of glaucomas
  • consecutive atrophy.
  • after retinochoroidal diseases
  • pigmentary retinopathy,
  • occlusions of the central retinal vein or artery

Optic nerve atrophies #22

  • Treatment
  • mostly sequelae of retinochoroidal diseases
  • no treatment
